n: A “new song” celebrates a fresh act of God’s goodness. This hymn is sung by the gathered “saints”—the faithful, covenant people—in public worship.

f.g: Hebrew ḥasidim—the faithful, loyal ones who keep covenant love (ḥesed) with God.

n: Israel is called to rejoice in the God who made them a people. He is not only their Creator but their King.
Worship here is joyful and physical: dancing, tambourines, and lyres. Israel’s praise could be full of movement and music, as when Miriam led the women after the Red Sea.

f.g: timbrel = a hand drum or tambourine.

n: The reason for joy: the Lord delights in his people and adorns the humble with salvation, like clothing them in beauty.
The faithful are to rejoice in the honor God gives them, singing even on their beds—praise that fills both public worship and private moments of night.

f.g: Here likely the honor or splendor God gives his people.

n: This verse pairs praise with a two-edged sword. Many think it reflects Israel’s early wars or a coming day of judgment. Christians have often read the sword spiritually, as the word of God.
The “vengeance” here is God’s justice on nations that oppressed his people, not personal revenge. Elsewhere scripture is clear that vengeance belongs to the Lord.

f.g: heathen = the nations, the peoples who did not know Israel’s God.

n: Proud kings and nobles who once bound Israel are now pictured bound themselves. It is a picture of reversal: the oppressors are brought under God’s rule.
The judgment is “written”—already decreed by God, not invented by people. To share in carrying out God’s righteous purposes is called an honor for all his faithful. The Hallelujah closes the psalm.

f.w: this honour have all his saints
